paragraphs: Yaʿqūb b. Efraim al-Shāmī[{2}] claimed that the people of Shām (Palestine) and the people of ʿIrāq (Babylonia) — despite the disagreement that exists between them — are both correct; and that God ordained worship by both schools at once, just as He ordained worship by two textual readings — that is, the Palestinian reading and the Babylonian reading of the Hebrew Bible. That is: we see that the people of ʿIrāq read with a textual recension different from the Palestinian recension, with differences in actual wording. We find that in one recension there is more: thus the Palestinian reads 2 Kgs 19:31, "the zeal of the Lord of Hosts shall perform this," and the Babylonian text lacks the word "of Hosts". Likewise the Palestinian reads Zech 14:4, "and his feet shall stand in that day on the Mount of Olives," and the Babylonian lacks "in that day." So if the Palestinian is right and the Babylonian is wrong, then there has been a deletion in the Babylonian. And if so, what guarantees us that, just as a deletion has occurred in the Babylonian copies (which are in the hands of a vast number of people), some additional deletions have not also occurred in the Palestinian copies — since they are in the hands of far fewer than those who read the Babylonian recension?

The Babylonian recension fills the world: from the border of al-Raqqa (Mesopotamia) to China in length and breadth; the bulk of those in the Arabian Peninsula, Khurāsān, Persia, ʿUmān, Iṣfahān, al-Jamāla, Bahrain, Yemen, and others. If something has dropped out of all of these hands, then a fortiori something must have dropped out of the Palestinian copies, which exist among a much smaller community. And if that is so, we cannot rule out that there have been deletions from the Book itself — of historical and legal substance. That — were it so — would be the demolition of religion. Moreover, prophets and saints lived in ʿIrāq — Ezekiel, Daniel, and others; and it is impossible that they would have used a reading and a language that God had not ordained for worship. Therefore God has ordained both readings; and if He has ordained two divergent textual recensions, He has likewise ordained two divergent halakhic schools. Since we observe that the transmitters have adopted both schools, we may conclude that God has ordained both of them.[{3}] ---
